title: Pooling standardized and unstandardized edges biases a component effect by exactly the untransported edges' share of the population difference
question: How large is the bias from pooling edges standardized to the target with edges left in their own populations, and is the two-stage route still the better practical choice than carrying every edge to the target?
design: Eight trials of one component, a quarter to three quarters with individual data, aggregate trials separated from the target by 0 to 1 SD, effect modification absent or present, continuous or binary outcome; two-stage marginal and conditional pooling against a transported alternative. 36 cells, 1000 replicates each.
answer: No. The two-stage bias equaled the aggregate edges' share of the pooled precision times the difference between their own-population and target effects (slope 0.97, R^2 0.997), zero only when modification or separation was zero. At 0.5 SD separation it reached -0.106 with coverage 0.27, and transporting every edge to the target had lower RMSE in all six such cells (0.038 to 0.089 against 0.047 to 0.113). Pooling conditional rather than marginal individual-data edges added up to 0.033 on the log odds ratio scale.
findings: b1 check: slope 0.967, intercept 0.0008, R^2 0.997 over 36 cells.
At 1 SD separation with a quarter of edges having individual data the two-stage bias exceeded the effect itself.
Transported arm coverage 0.90 to 0.96 (its variance ignores the shift's covariance with the individual-data edges); aggregate covariate laws were known exactly, so it is optimistic.
not_answered: Eight trials of one component rather than a component network; no one-stage component ML-NMR; aggregate covariate laws known; one network size. Peer review has not been done.
estimand: Marginal effect of one component in the target population
methods_compared: all edges transported to the target
